clinicalPearls: EA2 is an autosomal dominant channelopathy caused by loss-of-function mutations in CACNA1A, which encodes the pore-forming subunit of the neuronal P/Q-type (Cav2.1) voltage-gated calcium channel.
Attacks of ataxia with vertigo, nausea and dysarthria typically last hours to days, far longer than the seconds-to-minutes attacks of episodic ataxia type 1.
Common triggers include emotional or physical stress, exertion, fatigue, alcohol and caffeine.
Interictal downbeat or gaze-evoked nystagmus is a key clinical clue and is often present even between attacks.
Many patients respond well to acetazolamide, and 4-aminopyridine is a recognised alternative.
CACNA1A is allelic with familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 (gain-of-function change) and spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (a CAG repeat expansion), so migraine frequently coexists.
Over years a slowly progressive cerebellar syndrome with vermian atrophy may develop on top of the paroxysmal attacks.
In children, treatable metabolic causes of episodic ataxia must be excluded before settling on EA2.
reference.pathophysiology: Episodic ataxia type 2 is caused by heterozygous, usually loss-of-function, mutations in CACNA1A encoding the alpha-1A subunit of the neuronal P/Q-type (Cav2.1) voltage-gated calcium channel, which is densely expressed on cerebellar Purkinje and granule cells and at presynaptic terminals throughout the central nervous system. Reduced calcium current impairs cerebellar neuronal excitability and calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release, producing paroxysmal cerebellar dysfunction, while chronic channel dysfunction and slow Purkinje cell loss underlie the interictal nystagmus and the gradually progressive cerebellar atrophy seen in many patients. The therapeutic benefit of acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, is thought to reflect its effect on intracellular pH and neuronal excitability. The same gene illustrates striking allelic heterogeneity: gain-of-function missense changes cause familial hemiplegic migraine type 1, and an expanded CAG repeat causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 6, so overlapping migrainous and progressive ataxic features are common within CACNA1A disease.
additionalDifferentials: Episodic ataxia type 1 (KCNA1) with brief attacks and interictal neuromyotonia or myokymia
Other episodic ataxias and familial paroxysmal ataxic syndromes
Familial hemiplegic migraine and basilar-type migraine
Peripheral vestibular disorders such as vestibular migraine, Meniere disease and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Inherited metabolic episodic ataxias in children (for example pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, urea cycle and aminoacid disorders)
Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating disease
Posterior fossa structural lesion, Chiari malformation or vertebrobasilar ischaemia
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of CACNA1A including sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis
MRI of the brain to demonstrate cerebellar vermian atrophy and to exclude structural or demyelinating lesions
Careful examination for interictal downbeat or gaze-evoked nystagmus
A supervised therapeutic trial of acetazolamide, where a clear response supports the diagnosis
Metabolic screening in children including lactate, ammonia, plasma amino acids and urine organic acids
Audiovestibular testing when vertigo is a prominent feature
redFlags: A progressive fixed cerebellar deficit or new focal neurological signs suggesting a structural lesion
Prolonged hemiplegia or impaired consciousness overlapping with severe hemiplegic migraine within CACNA1A disease
Attacks accompanied by seizures or reduced consciousness that require broader evaluation
Sudden severe headache or posterior circulation stroke features
reference.prognosis: Attacks often respond well to acetazolamide with preserved function between episodes, but many patients develop a slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia with persistent nystagmus over decades. Overall the disorder is compatible with a normal lifespan.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the paroxysmal attacks as functional or psychogenic, or as simple vestibular migraine.
Overlooking interictal nystagmus, which is a strong pointer to the diagnosis.
Confusing EA2 with episodic ataxia type 1, which is distinguished by much shorter attacks and myokymia.
Failing to recognise the allelic overlap with hemiplegic migraine and spinocerebellar ataxia type 6.
Missing treatable inherited metabolic mimics in children presenting with episodic ataxia.
references: Principles and practice of medical genetics
management: Offer acetazolamide as the mainstay prophylaxis, which often markedly reduces attacks, with 4-aminopyridine as a recognised alternative
Advise avoidance of triggers including emotional or physical stress, exertion, fatigue, alcohol and caffeine
Manage coexisting migraine, which frequently accompanies the disorder given the allelic relationship with familial hemiplegic migraine
Provide vestibular rehabilitation for vertigo and nystagmus, with falls-prevention measures
Monitor over time for slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia and vermian atrophy
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant CACNA1A inheritance and arrange family screening, coordinated through neurology and clinical genetics
